title: Green Cards Reflect Cases Started Years Ago: Attorney's Five-Point Rebuttal
excerpt: Gnanamookan Senthurjothi's five points: green cards issued today trace to 2013–2014 filings, PERM already protects laid-off Americans, and arithmetic is not evidence.
body:
• Immigration attorney Gnanamookan Senthurjothi has laid out five points challenging the Trump administration's claim that green-card numbers prove tech firms replaced American workers with foreign staff.
  • His centerpiece argument: Indians receiving employment-based green cards today filed their cases around 2013–2014 — approvals now reflect decade-old relationships, not recent hiring.
  • PERM already contains a displacement safeguard, he says: employers that laid off US workers in the same occupation within six months of filing must notify and consider them.
  • What this means for you: if your employer is among the suspended eight, you can keep working on your current H-1B — only new and pending PERM filings are frozen. If your I-140 is already approved, AC21 rules let you extend H-1B status past the six-year cap. Attorneys expect lawsuits against the suspensions within days; get competent counsel before switching jobs or making travel plans.

Vice President JD Vance's arithmetic looked damning at first glance: 6,000 American workers laid off at Microsoft, alongside 6,300 H-1B visas and nearly 3,000 green cards. Immigration attorney Gnanamookan Senthurjothi says the numbers are real — and nearly meaningless as evidence. In a five-point rebuttal circulating this week, he argues the administration has conflated distinct processes, timelines and job roles into a replacement narrative the evidence does not support.

"Layoffs and approvals can fall in the same reporting period without involving the same jobs, teams or individuals," Senthurjothi said, according to Times Now World. His message to the administration: "The numbers may justify asking questions. They do not, by themselves, answer them."

The five points

One: H-1B approvals are not new hires. A large share of filings are extensions or status changes for people already employed. Microsoft's own disclosure is the exhibit: roughly 80% of its nearly 6,000 H-1B filings last fiscal year covered existing employees, not recruits arriving from abroad. Counting approvals as arrivals, Senthurjothi says, is a category error.

Two: roles are not interchangeable. Terminating an employee in one department does not create a vacancy a foreign worker fills. Because roles, skill sets and team responsibilities vary significantly, he argues, specific evidence about individual job functions is required before any displacement claim can stand. Headcount in, headcount out is not proof of substitution.

Three: green cards are decade-old cases. The employment-based queue for Indians is so long that people receiving green cards now initiated their applications around 2013–2014. "So 3,000 green cards now does not mean they have been hired now," Senthurjothi said. Most employment-based green cards go to workers already with the sponsoring employer, often for years, with the PERM labor certification filed long before final approval.

Four: displacement safeguards already exist. Under PERM rules, an employer that laid off US workers in the same or a related occupation within six months before filing must notify and consider those workers. The system, he says, already contains the remedy the administration claims is missing.

Five: investigate with evidence, not arithmetic. Senthurjothi concedes the Labor Department is entitled to investigate suspected violations — and says it should, if employers made false certifications or unlawfully disadvantaged American workers. But "the evidence should determine the consequences," not statistical correlation.

Diaspora Angle

For Indian professionals, the rebuttal reframes the fear. The workers in the crosshairs are not recent arrivals gaming a loophole — many are people who have worked for the same employer for a decade, paid taxes, and waited out the longest green-card backlog in the system. That framing matters legally too: attorneys expect the suspensions to face court challenges arguing the administration overstepped its authority, with federal law permitting only a 180-day unilateral pause per employer pending investigation.

What's Next / Looking Ahead

The practical fallout is immediate. Pending PERM cases from the eight suspended employers are on hold, and because PERM recruitment generally must lead to a filing within 180 days, a prolonged freeze could force employers to restart labor-market tests — stalling priority dates for workers deep in the backlog. Business Insider's reporting has attorneys predicting lawsuits "by next week," and advising worried workers to seek counsel now: do not self-deport on rumor, do not make irreversible travel plans, and document your status. The administration's numbers, Senthurjothi's five points suggest, have opened an argument — they have not closed one.

Displacement safeguards are already in place.
Investigate with evidence, not just numbers.
